etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English moral, from Old French moral, from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”) (first used by Cicero, to translate Ancient Greek ἠθικός (ēthikós, “moral”)), from mos (“manner, custom”).

definitions.definition: Of or relating to principles of right and wrong in behaviour, especially for teaching right behaviour.

quote.citation: 1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne, The Scarlet Letter, a Romance, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, →OCLC:
quote.text: She had wandered without rule or guidance in a moral wilderness.

definitions.definition: Conforming to a standard of right behaviour; sanctioned by or operative on one's conscience or ethical judgment.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter I, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The stories did not seem to me to touch life. They were plainly intended to have a bracing moral effect, and perhaps had this result for the people at whom they were aimed. They left me with the impression of a well-delivered stereopticon lecture, with characters about as life-like as the shadows on the screen, and whisking on and off, at the mercy of the operator.

definitions.definition: Capable of right and wrong action.
Positively affecting the mind, confidence, or will.
(of a narrative) The ethical significance or practical lesson.

quote.citation: 1841, Thomas Macaulay, Comic Dramatists of the Restoration (printed in Edinburgh Review, January 1841)
quote.text: We protest against the principle that the world of pure comedy is one into which no moral enters.

definitions.definition: (chiefly in the plural) Moral practices or teachings: modes of conduct.
(of a media) A depiction of good or heroic actions.
